1.explanation: Both src/languages/python.js and python-repl.js define the Python grammar (including number and keyword regexes). The Python mode in python.js is where the ‘number’ pattern is currently too permissive (it’s matching letters after digits), preventing the keyword patterns (which rely on word boundaries) from firing. The REPL wrapper reuses the same number logic. Editing these files to tighten the number regex (so it stops at the end of the digit) and/or adjust keyword boundary assertions will resolve the issue.
1.bug_scenario: When Python code is highlighted with highlight.js, number tokens like “1if” in “print(1if 0==0else\"b\")” are being consumed as a single “number” token, so the keywords “if” and “else” aren’t recognized. The images show that “1if” and “0else” are all green (number) instead of splitting into a number followed by an ‘if’ or ‘else’ keyword. The expected behavior is to tokenize “1” as a number and “if” as a keyword (and similarly for “else”), matching GitHub’s own Python highlighting.

2.explanation:
• src/languages/python.js contains the NUMBER and keyword definitions for Python. Its number regex is currently too permissive (it doesn’t enforce a word-boundary after the digits), so it swallows adjacent letters and prevents the ‘if’/‘else’ patterns from ever matching.  
• src/languages/python-repl.js reuses the same core Python modes (including the faulty number/keyword logic) in REPL contexts, so it exhibits the same issue and must be patched in parallel.  
• src/lib/compile_keywords.js builds the keyword-matching regex for all languages. It doesn’t wrap the generated keyword pattern in the proper look-arounds or word-boundary checks, so keywords can only match if they start on their own token boundary. Tightening these patterns (adding \b or negative look-arounds around keywords) will prevent number modes from bleeding into our keywords.
2.bug_scenario: In Python highlighting, when a keyword (for example “if” or “else”) immediately follows a number literal without any whitespace (e.g. “1if” or “0else”), the highlighter treats the entire string as one big number token, so the keyword never gets recognized. The screenshots show that “1if” and “0else” are green (number) tokens instead of splitting into a number (1) followed by the keyword (if).
